doc.title: Virginia Mayhew interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 23, 2022

title: Name that tune: her composition 'Monterey Blues'
summary: Rowe hums a tune in five that she identifies as her own 'Monterey Blues'; they talk about the adaptable blues form and Monk tunes in odd meters.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Let me try a name this tune on you.
Oh goodness. I’m so bad at remembering the name of tunes. Are you going to play something for me?
Well I’m so bad at trying to vocalize it so let me just get my [hums]. [Scats] wait hold on. [Scats]. Supposed to be in five.
Oh okay.
Have you got it?
One-two-three-
[Scats]
Oh yeah. “Monterey Blues.”
You got it, yay. You move on to the next round.
Boy you sure do your homework for these things.
Well I love that tune and it’s a great way to play something in five that still feels good.
It’s still cheerful.
It’s still cheerful.

Yeah. I agree. I agree that they don’t play anything in five like that these days. I’m so old, I mean I feel just like what happened? Twenty years ago there were a lot of people that felt — anyhow whatever.
Well for the people who watch this I should mention that that’s a composition of yours. Right?
Yes. “Monterey Blues.”
And it’s interesting that we’ve been talking about the blues and I just love the fact that the blues form is so adaptable. You can just never stop using it. You can put anything to it.
Yep. Mess with it. Another — you know Monk tunes are also really good for that. Monk tunes, because they’re so strong.
Yeah.
The melodies or the rhythms, you know the hits and stuff, they work really well with odd meters or —
